extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers/physicians, anatomists, and Royal Society readers (17th‑century experimental scientists)
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and arguing for anatomical and physiological hypotheses by combining dissections, microscopic observation, case reports, quantitative estimates, and responses to objections. Emphasises experimental demonstration and detailed specimen preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical ocular demonstration over theoretical objection
rubrics_metrics.description: When structural objections are raised (e.g., that the Fallopian tubes are too narrow to transmit eggs), the author insists ocular demonstration by dissection is decisive: 'the eggs are discovered in the entrance, and afterward to have made their way through them into the womb.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer direct dissection/observation to settle anatomical controversies; report clear, observed locations of structures (e.g., eggs in tubes and their passage) to refute purely structural arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed case reporting for clinical phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Clinical cases should include a full timeline of signs, attempted interventions, changes in behaviour, witness reports, and ultimate outcome (e.g., the rabies patient: attempts to drink, convulsions, boluses, clyster, death; witness accounts about preceding tremors and the dog).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give sequential detail (what was tried, patient posture and responses, timing of events, treatments and their immediate effects), and include collateral testimony when relevant to causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical correlation of function (optic nerve fibres & vision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue physiological function by correlating anatomy with clinical phenomena: optic nerve fibres (origin, tension, order) are more concerned in vision than cornea/humours/retina, supported by amaurosis cases where ocular parts appear normal but sight is lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dissection and clinical-pathological correlation to support claims about which structures 'perform' sensation; describe origins, relative tension, and positional relations of fibres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate objections and answer by experiment or appeal to experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond to conceivable objections (e.g., how soft fibres could have tension; why top fibres would produce different acuity) by experiment, analogy, and empirical appeals: spider's web analogy, Lord Bacon's experiment, personal appeals to reading experience and eye position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state foreseeable objections, then provide experiments, analogies, or simple sensory tests (e.g., reading position, observing pupil accommodation) to rebut them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for preparing retina for microscopic inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparing the retina by putting it in water is intended 'not to wash off the mucous substance... but to expand the fibres by the playing it up and down in warm water, and to magnify the image of it by a double refraction of the lucid rays.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe preparation steps and purpose (warm water agitation to expand fibres, use of a glass to magnify via refraction), and warn about misinterpretation (it's not to remove proper mucous substance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of eye‑position and accommodation observations as experimental evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use observable changes in pupil position and ease of seeing (e.g., characters read better held below the eye than above; right eye accommodating to left when viewing a near lateral object) as experimental support for anatomy-based claims about fibre tension and correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include simple behavioural/visual experiments and reports of what an observer will see (pupil turning, convergence/divergence) as evidence for anatomical-function hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough anatomical description in dissections (including anomalies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissections should enumerate all notable anatomical findings (e.g., absence of bladder/uterus, ureters inserted into rectum, rectum sealed like a bladder) and note uncertainty about causes (natural or iatrogenic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record both normal and anomalous structures precisely, note measurements/relationships (e.g., insertion distances), and discuss possible interpretations without overstating causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative description and calculation for physiological processes (plants)
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing vascular/physiological processes in plants, provide quantitative counts and estimates (e.g., number of vessels per square inch, drops transported, converting to cubic feet and weight) to support functional claims like sap transport capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include counting methods, assumptions (drops per vessel per day, conversion factors), and stepwise calculations so readers can assess the estimate's plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopic and sectional methodology for wood anatomy
rubrics_metrics.description: To characterise wood vessels and rings, saw and plane a cross-section smooth, cut longwise and across to reveal ascending and horizontal vessels, and use magnifying glasses/microscopes to distinguish vessel types and partitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe which cuts (cross vs longwise) reveal which structures; indicate magnification used and how features (bladders, partitions/valves) appear under the instrument; comment on variability across species (oak vs elm vs beech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative literature and authorship to situate findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Situate observations with respect to prior work (e.g., cite Harvey, de Graaf, Grew, Malpighi, Bacon, Newton), noting where earlier observers were 'near' discoveries or where your observations confirm/refine theirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly reference prior authorities, explain how current observations confirm, contradict, or extend them, and use that context to strengthen interpretative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish description from speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate straightforward anatomical/experimental description from broader speculations: the author omits some speculations on a case as 'tending to throw little light on the subject' and elsewhere notes when conjectures are being made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label speculative remarks clearly and avoid presenting conjecture as demonstrated fact; prioritize empirical description and reserve speculation for clearly indicated discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer function from structural arrangement and comparative tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer differences of function (e.g., superior vs inferior optic fibres tension) from structural arrangement and observable impressions when nerves are drawn, asserting that superior fibres 'press more on the subjacent medullary protuberances' and make a deeper impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support functional inferences with direct manipulation/observation of structures (e.g., drawing out nerves) and report tactile or visible signs (pressure impressions) as evidence.
